interpretations.rationale: The question is whether a future handed back by VerifyLeader, Barrier or Apply around Shutdown can be left permanently uncompleted, and the corrected revision now answers it with all five declared comparisons satisfied, including the two that a configuration change makes decisive. A call made after Shutdown has returned should get the documented 'raft is already shutdown' error, and that is what happens for the unbuffered call kinds: Barrier and Apply answered all eight post-shutdown calls in every trial (comparisons 2 and 3, indices 3, 9, 15 and 5, 11, 17). VerifyLeader, whose channel is always buffered, answered only 4, 4 and 5 of its eight post-shutdown calls (indices 1, 7 and 13), leaving 4, 4 and 3 futures incomplete after 500ms. With BatchApplyCh enabled - the option whose comment says it buffers applyCh to MaxAppendEntries and thereby breaks the timeout guarantee on Apply - the two unbuffered kinds flip: Barrier answered 6, 3 and 4 of eight (indices 25, 29, 33) and Apply 3, 3 and 5 (indices 27, 31, 35), leaving 11 and 13 of 24 calls stranded respectively, with roughly half of the calls in each case answered and the rest left with a future nothing will complete (comparisons 0 and 1). That is a causal rather than correlational demonstration: the only difference between the answered and the stranded cases is whether the channel a future is sent to is buffered, since the call shape, the future type and the absence of a shutdown channel on these futures are identical. The source explains the split exactly: VerifyLeader and the apply path share the same select over the shutdown channel and a channel send, verifyCh is created with 64 slots while applyCh is unbuffered unless BatchApplyCh buffers it, and none of these futures sets ShutdownCh, so deferError.Error() waits on an error channel that no surviving goroutine will write. The repository's own test file records the same class as a TODO for these calls, which is an admission that the gap was known rather than a contract that permits a caller's Error() to block forever. The earlier receipts stay part of the account: the first showed the racing form, 9 and 41 of 64 futures incomplete in two of three trials with none in the control, and the two later revisions did not reproduce that form (0 of 128 per case), so the racing variant is a timing-dependent manifestation while the post-shutdown form is stable across three executions and is the one the claim rests on. A fifth revision tested whether the strand depends on spare capacity in verifyCh by issuing 320 concurrent racing calls, five times the 64 slots, in three VerifyLeader cases (result events at parsed indices 25, 27 and 29). Over-subscription did not protect later callers: 6, 5 and 6 of the eight post-shutdown calls were answered and 2, 3 and 2 returned futures that stayed incomplete, which is the same outcome as the 128-call cases in the same run (5, 1 and 3 answered; 3, 7 and 5 stranded) and the declared comparison asking for every post-shutdown call to be answered was therefore contradicted with three valid witnesses. The reading is that the racing surplus senders are released by the shutdown case instead of holding slots, so the buffer ends partially empty at the exit and later callers still find a free slot to be accepted into; occupancy at the exit is thus not what decides the strand, and the mechanism stands as the buffered channel plus a future with no shutdown channel of its own.
counterevidence: The racing form did not reproduce in the later revisions (0 of 128 calls per case in two runs), so the earlier 9 and 41 are a timing-dependent manifestation rather than a rate.

Without BatchApplyCh the apply path is never affected: Barrier and Apply answered every post-shutdown call in all three runs (indices 3, 9, 15 and 5, 11, 17 here), so the defect reaches the apply path only under a configuration whose own comment already warns that it breaks the Apply timeout guarantee.

Roughly half of the calls in each affected case are answered with the documented shutdown error rather than stranded, so the outcome is a per-call select choice, and no call that was answered carried a wrong outcome.
The repository's test file records the same class as a known TODO, which is evidence about intent, not a reason to treat an unbounded block as acceptable.

The strand is classified by a 500ms window; permanence is inferred from the source, since no reader of the affected channel remains and these futures carry no shutdown channel.

knowledge.statement: VerifyLeader counts acknowledgements from non-voters toward a voter-sized quorum, so it can report success for an interval in which the leader has had no successful interaction with any other voter. verifyLeader registers every entry of leaderState.replState (which startStopReplication creates for every configured server except the leader itself, without consulting Suffrage) on repl.notify, so each of those peers is asked to acknowledge; a successful AppendEntries reply (updateLastAppended and the heartbeat path) or a successful InstallSnapshot replies with notifyAll(true), which calls verifyFuture.vote(true) and increments votes; the threshold compared against is quorumSize(), computed as (voters in configurations.latest)/2+1. Every other leadership-quorum test in the same package restricts eligibility to voters: checkLeaderLease skips non-voter servers in its contacted count and requestVote rejects a candidate without a vote, so the two leadership tests disagree about whose support counts.
knowledge.conditions: A leader whose latest configuration (configurations.latest) contains a server with Suffrage other than Voter, and which can still exchange AppendEntries or InstallSnapshot RPCs with that server. With three voters and one non-voter, quorumSize() is 2, so the leader's own vote plus one non-voter acknowledgement reaches the threshold.

knowledge.statement: The leader's own leadership lease is computed over voters only: checkLeaderLease counts itself plus those servers in configurations.latest whose Suffrage is Voter and whose followerReplication last contact is within LeaderLeaseTimeout, and steps down when that count is below quorumSize(). A leader therefore stops counting an unreachable voter as contacted and steps down within roughly LeaderLeaseTimeout of the last successful interaction, while a follower cannot campaign before ElectionTimeout has elapsed since it last heard from a leader.
knowledge.conditions: A configuration accepted by Config.Validate, which requires 5ms <= LeaderLeaseTimeout <= HeartbeatTimeout <= ElectionTimeout; the lease check is driven by the leader's own timer and by the last-contact times its replication goroutines record.

knowledge.statement: Runtime configuration reload enforces the same timeout bounds as initial construction: ReloadConfig applies the reloadable fields onto the current configuration and returns the error from ValidateConfig before storing it, so LeaderLeaseTimeout can never exceed HeartbeatTimeout, nor HeartbeatTimeout exceed ElectionTimeout, on a running node. A leader cannot therefore be given a longer lease than a follower's election timeout through the public reload API.
knowledge.conditions: A call to Raft.ReloadConfig on a running node with a protocol-supported configuration; the check is performed under r.confReloadMu before the new configuration is stored, and on failure the previous configuration remains in force.

knowledge.statement: LeadershipTransferToServer accepts a non-voter target and reports success without transferring leadership to it. The leader resolves the requested ID in leaderState.replState, which contains an entry for every configured server except the leader (startStopReplication creates one per server without consulting Suffrage) and only errors with 'cannot find replication state' when no entry exists. The selected target is sent TimeoutNow, which sets it to Candidate and marks candidateFromLeadershipTransfer; that flag makes runCandidate skip pre-vote, so the target sends a real RequestVote carrying the next term. A voter handling that request adopts the higher term and becomes a follower before it reaches the hasVote check, which then refuses the vote because the candidate holds no vote; the candidate therefore cannot win. When the old leader observes the higher term it steps down, the transfer goroutine's leftLeaderLoop branch responds nil, and the caller sees success. By contrast LeadershipTransfer with no explicit target picks through pickServer, which skips every server whose Suffrage is not Voter.
knowledge.conditions: Protocol version >= 3 (otherwise LeadershipTransferToServer returns ErrUnsupportedProtocol), a cluster whose latest configuration at the leader contains the named server with Suffrage other than Voter, and pre-vote enabled or disabled (the transfer path skips pre-vote either way). The named server must be reachable from the leader, otherwise the leader reports a TimeoutNow failure instead.

knowledge.statement: A leadership transfer requested for a non-voter leaves the cluster without a leader until a voter wins the next election, while the call itself has already reported success. In the observed run with HeartbeatTimeout = ElectionTimeout = LeaderLeaseTimeout = 200ms, the call returned nil, the requested non-voter was never Leader, the previous leader was sampled outside Leader state in all 1289 samples from the instant of the call, 241 samples found no leader at all (first 1ms, last 278ms after the call, about 1.4 election timeouts), the maximum term rose from 2 to 4, and a different voter held leadership at the end. The voter-target control with the same call returned nil and did hand leadership to the requested server.
knowledge.conditions: Cluster of three voters plus one non-voter joined through AddNonvoter, protocol version >= 3, all peers reachable, pre-vote left at its default, and a single process with in-memory transports; the target is chosen by its suffrage in the leader's latest configuration, not by any observed result.

knowledge.statement: Election vote solicitation is restricted to voters, unlike the verify path in the same file. electSelf and preElectSelf both iterate configurations.latest.Servers and act only when server.Suffrage == Voter: the local server records a vote for itself and every other server is asked with a RequestVote or RequestPreVote RPC, while non-voters are skipped altogether, so no non-voter grant is ever counted toward the voter-sized quorum they compare against. The grant side is not what keeps non-voters out: requestVote rejects a candidate that holds no vote and a candidate that is not in the configuration, but it imposes no suffrage requirement on the server granting, and it persists and grants a vote whenever the candidate's log is at least as up to date, so a non-voter would grant if it were asked. verifyLeader is the path that does ask every entry of leaderState.replState, which includes non-voters.
knowledge.conditions: A server whose latest configuration contains non-voting members, with pre-vote either enabled (preElectSelf) or disabled (electSelf directly); the solicitation loops read configurations.latest on the candidate's own main thread.

knowledge.statement: A follower attempts an election after HeartbeatTimeout without contact from a leader, and ElectionTimeout governs only a candidate's retry. runFollower arms heartbeatTimer with randomTimeout(HeartbeatTimeout) and campaigns when the time since last contact is at least HeartbeatTimeout, while runCandidate arms its timer with randomTimeout(ElectionTimeout) and simply restarts the election when it fires. randomTimeout(v) returns v plus a random fraction of v, so a campaign begins in [H, 2H). Correspondingly ValidateConfig requires LeaderLeaseTimeout <= HeartbeatTimeout <= ElectionTimeout, and the leader's own lease check runs every max(minCheckInterval, LeaderLeaseTimeout - maxDiff) with minCheckInterval = 10ms, stepping down at the first check whose voter contact age exceeds LeaderLeaseTimeout; the comparison is diff <= leaseTimeout, so a check at exactly the boundary still counts the voter as contacted.
knowledge.conditions: The default follower and leader loops in this snapshot, with pre-vote enabled or disabled; the numbers quoted are for a configuration accepted by ValidateConfig, and the exposure analysis assumes in-memory or low-latency RPCs.

knowledge.statement: A VerifyLeader request queued while a leader's main loop is stalled past its lease is answered without success once the stall ends, even though a successor has been elected in the meantime. Across eight trials the stalled leader held only Leader state for every 1ms sample while another server led at term 3 (first seen at 345-464ms), yet the queued verify returned non-nil in all eight: seven times 'leadership lost while committing log' and twice 'node is not the leader', at 600-602ms, the moment the stall released the main loop; the concurrent Apply failed the same way. The endpoints show the lease case was already ready when the loop resumed, so leadership was given up before the non-voter's acknowledgement could be counted, which is ordering rather than the eligibility rule that the verify quorum itself violates.
knowledge.conditions: Three voters plus one non-voter, the leader partitioned so only the non-voter is reachable, HeartbeatTimeout = ElectionTimeout = LeaderLeaseTimeout = 200ms, a 600ms stall that blocks StoreLogs on the leader's main thread while a client Apply is in flight, in-memory transports in one process.

knowledge.statement: A leader whose main loop is stalled past its lease can return VerifyLeader success while a successor already leads the cluster at a higher term, because the acknowledgement it counts arrives on a replication goroutine and the lease check that would have removed it runs on the stalled main loop. In the retained run the old leader stayed at term 2 while another server led at term 3 from 319-454ms; all six trials sampled a successor before the verdict, and in three of them (parsed indices 3, 7 and 9) the leader's VerifyLeader returned success at 931ms, the moment the 900ms store stall released the loop and the already-counted non-voter acknowledgement was delivered; the other three answered 'leadership lost while committing log'.
knowledge.conditions: Three voters plus one non-voter; the leader isolated from both other voters and from the non-voter while the request is registered; the leader's main loop then blocked inside StoreLogs for 900ms by a client Apply; the non-voter reconnected 250-500ms later; HeartbeatTimeout = ElectionTimeout = LeaderLeaseTimeout = 200ms, in-memory transports in one process.

interpretations.rationale: VerifyLeader's documented role is to ensure this peer is still the leader so that stale data is not returned from the FSM. The source trace shows the guarantee is weaker than that role requires: the confirming votes are gathered from every replication peer, including non-voters, while the threshold is a voter quorum. With three voters and one non-voter, quorumSize() is 2, so the leader's own vote plus a single non-voter acknowledgement reaches the threshold and VerifyLeader returns nil; the same code gives the non-voter no standing in checkLeaderLease's lease count or in a vote request, so the two leadership tests disagree about whose support counts. The consequence for reads is bounded rather than unconditional: checkLeaderLease uses voters only, so under a validated configuration the lease normally removes the old leader before a voter majority can elect a successor, and the acknowledgements counted while the leader is still legitimately leader are not themselves stale. The account therefore asserts a defect in the decision support VerifyLeader provides (success without voter-majority acknowledgement) and treats the stale-read consequence as conditional on the lease's timing assumption (a leader stall, clock jump or lease check interleaving that lets a successor be elected while the old leader still reports success). The requested probe fixes the acknowledging peer's identity independently of the result: the partition, not the outcome, selects the peer, and the non-voter is joined through the leader's own AddNonvoter path.
counterevidence: checkLeaderLease counts voters only, so a leader that has lost voter-majority contact steps down within about LeaderLeaseTimeout; this bounds the stale-read consequence rather than showing VerifyLeader's decision support to be adequate.

interpretations.rationale: The question asked whether a leader stalled past its lease can still answer a queued VerifyLeader with success by counting the reachable non-voter, and the execution answers no for this model. The queued VerifyLeader nevertheless never reported success: every endpoint was non-nil, seven trials answering 'leadership lost while committing log' and two answering 'node is not the leader', all at 600-602ms, which is exactly when the 600ms store stall released the main loop. The same run's Apply in the same window also ended with ErrLeadershipLost. The endpoints distinguish the two interleavings: 'leadership lost while committing log' is the answer the leader loop's cleanup gives to a verify it has already registered, so in those trials the verify case was served and then the runLeader defer answered it when leadership was given up, while 'node is not the leader' is the follower loop's answer to a request still queued in verifyCh, so in those trials the request never even reached verifyLeader. Neither outcome counts the non-voter's acknowledgement. The reason is ordering rather than eligibility: by the time the stall ends, the lease case is already ready, so the main loop gives up leadership in the next iteration, before the heartbeat round trip to the non-voter can return a vote. This refutes the suspicion for this route, not the parent defect: the accounting behaviour that counts a non-voter remains in the source and was observed directly in the parent question's probe. What the trial excludes is the specific consequence I was probing, namely that a stalled leader serving a queued verify hands a client a stale-read verdict. The parent question's gap therefore narrows to that scheduling residue rather than closing.
counterevidence: The stall model, not the source, is what the trials refute: a slower or differently placed stall could change which case the main loop serves first, and a networked deployment makes each RPC round trip orders of magnitude slower than the loop iteration, which is the opposite direction from the one that produced these endpoints.

In two trials the failure was ErrNotLeader rather than ErrLeadershipLost, showing the queued request sometimes never reached verifyLeader at all; those trials measure the queue being drained after leadership loss rather than the race between the acknowledgement and the step-down.
limitations: One execution of eight trials is cited; the endpoints were uniform (0/8 success) but the reported interleavings are inferred from the two error values, not sampled directly.

interpretations.rationale: The question was whether a future handed back by VerifyLeader, Barrier or Apply while Shutdown runs can be left permanently uncompleted, and the execution answers yes for VerifyLeader. In the retained run of three shutdown trials (result events at parsed indices 1, 7 and 13) the verify cases left 9, 41 and 0 of their 64 futures uncompleted 400ms after Shutdown() had returned, with every completed call reporting success; the same call kind on a node that is never shut down completed all 64 in its control (index 19). So 50 of 192 verify calls were still waiting long after the node had reported Shutdown complete, and nothing is left that could answer them: Shutdown closes shutdownCh and sets the state to Shutdown (api.go 1060-1072), the run loop and the FSM goroutine both exit on that channel, and the futures sit in verifyCh, a buffered channel of 64 (api.go 576) that nobody drains afterwards. That matches the source: VerifyLeader creates a verifyFuture and calls init(), which allocates only the error channel (future.go 99-101), leaving ShutdownCh nil, so deferError.Error() waits on errCh or on a channel that is never used (future.go 103-117). The contract names ErrRaftShutdown as an error a client may see from these calls, and the repository's own test file already carries a TODO that Barrier, VerifyLeader and GetConfiguration can get stuck when the buffered channel consumes a future that shutdown then never processes (raft_test.go 38-42). The exposure is timing dependent rather than uniform: the third verify trial left nothing behind, and the run's other two call kinds never left a future incomplete at all (Barrier 0 of 192 across indices 3, 9, 15; Apply 0 of 192 across 5, 11, 17). That difference is consistent with how the loop drains each channel: it takes one case per iteration from verifyCh, whereas applyCh is drained in batches up to MaxAppendEntries in the group-commit loop, so a queue of apply or barrier futures is emptied before the shutdown case is chosen far more reliably. The mechanism itself does not require many callers: any single VerifyLeader whose send wins the select while the loop is exiting lands in the buffer and stays there, but the likelihood that the buffer is non-empty at that moment grows with concurrent callers, which is what the probe exercises.
counterevidence: One of the three verify trials left no future uncompleted, and the two other call kinds never did in 384 attempts, so the outcome is a race whose probability depends on queue occupancy at the exit rather than a deterministic property of the API.

interpretations.rationale: VerifyLeader's documented role is to ensure this peer is still the leader so that stale data is not returned from the FSM. The question was whether its success establishes voter-majority contact; the execution says it does not. In the retained run of the three-partition probe, the leader whose only reachable peer was the non-voter returned success in 0ms while its own latest configuration reported three voters, one non-voter and a quorum size of 2, and the leader was still in Leader state (parsed event index 1); the control partition that kept one voter reachable also returned success, which shows the harness does observe a genuine acknowledgement path (index 3); the control partition with no reachable peer did not return success at all, returning 'leadership lost while committing log' after 202ms with the node in Follower state, so the leader cannot reach the threshold on its own vote and the non-voter acknowledgement is what satisfied it in the first case (index 5). All three declared comparisons hold with the setup event matched as admission (correlations 1->0, 3->2, 5->4). The source explains the mechanism: verifyLeader asks every entry of leaderState.replState to acknowledge, startStopReplication creates such an entry for every configured server except the leader without consulting Suffrage, any successful AppendEntries or InstallSnapshot reply from such a peer calls notifyAll(true) and increments verifyFuture.votes, and the threshold compared against is quorumSize(), counted over voters alone. The same package treats voter eligibility strictly in its other leadership tests: checkLeaderLease does not count a non-voter, requestVote refuses a candidate that holds no vote, and quorumSize itself counts only voters, so the verify path is the outlier rather than a deliberate relaxation. The consequence for reads stays bounded and is not what this receipt measures. The leader's lease is voter-only, and both Config.Validate and ReloadConfig enforce LeaderLeaseTimeout <= HeartbeatTimeout <= ElectionTimeout, so the old leader is normally removed before a voter majority elects a successor; the no-peer control is exactly that lease firing at 202ms with a 200ms lease. What the receipt does establish is the weaker but unconditional part: for an interval in which the leader exchanged nothing with any other voter, VerifyLeader reports success, so a caller relying on that call for read consistency is really relying on the lease timer rather than on the acknowledgements VerifyLeader collected. The same file shows the omission is not a considered relaxation of voter eligibility: electSelf and preElectSelf build the very same voter-sized threshold, and both iterate the leader's latest configuration asking only servers whose Suffrage is Voter, so a candidate neither solicits nor counts a non-voter's grant even though nothing on the granting side stops a non-voter from granting a vote if it were asked. Only the verify path asks every replication peer. That contrast is recorded as its own Behaviour so the finding is not reused without it, and it turns the question's answer from 'the success signal is weaker than its documentation' into 'the success signal contradicts the eligibility rule the same decisions use everywhere else'. The consequence that this account previously kept conditional is now witnessed. A separate probe registers the verify request while the leader is isolated from every peer, stalls the leader's main loop inside StoreLogs for 900ms so its lease case cannot run, and reconnects only the non-voter once a voter majority has had time to elect. In all six trials a different server was sampled in Leader state at term 3 before the verdict (first at 319-454ms) while the old leader stayed at term 2, and in three of them (result events at parsed indices 3, 7 and 9) the old leader's VerifyLeader returned success at 931ms - the moment the stall released the loop, by which time the non-voter's acknowledgement had already been counted on a replication goroutine. The other three trials answered 'leadership lost while committing log', so the outcome is a per-trial choice between the two ready cases, but the successful ones are exactly the stale-read verdict the API says it prevents: a caller told 'still leader' while a successor already led at a higher term. Two details keep this from contradicting the earlier refuted child question, which asked whether a request *queued during* the stall can succeed: it cannot, because the main loop must be running to register the request, and that is why the successful construction registers first and stalls afterwards. The parent defect claim is unchanged; what changes is its consequence, which is no longer conditional on an unobserved interleaving but demonstrated under a stated condition.

counterevidence: The leadership lease still bounds the ordinary case: without a stalled main loop the lease case is served no later than LeaderLeaseTimeout, which is why the six-trial probe needed a 900ms store stall to reach the condition.

Only three of the six trials returned success; the other three answered leadership loss, so the verdict is a per-trial choice between the ready verify case and the ready lease case rather than a deterministic outcome.

The witness depends on a non-voter in the configuration and reachable from the stalled leader; the earlier controls show that without any acknowledgement the same call fails (no-peer control) and that a voter acknowledgement is the legitimate path.
The stalled leader never adopted the successor's term (leader_term_after stayed 2 in every trial), which is what makes the two leaders coexist and the verdict stale.
limitations: The stall is a wrapper around the log store that blocks StoreLogs on the leader's main thread, and the non-voter is reconnected by transport calls; both are supplied conditions rather than faults observed in a deployment.

The verdict arrives when the stall releases the main loop (931-932ms in every trial), so the success is returned at the first loop iteration after the acknowledgement had already been counted, not while the loop was blocked.

The caller's subsequent read of the FSM is not exercised; the stale-read consequence is that the API's documented purpose ('to prevent returning stale data from the FSM') is not met, which the witness establishes from the endpoint and the concurrent successor rather than from a data read.

result.summary: Interpreted the over-subscription revision, which refutes the occupancy explanation rather than the defect. With 320 concurrent racing calls against 64 verifyCh slots, the post-shutdown strand persisted: 6, 5 and 6 of eight calls answered and 2, 3 and 2 left incomplete, versus 5, 1 and 3 answered with 3, 7 and 5 stranded in the 128-call cases from the same run, so the declared prediction that over-subscribing would answer every later call was contradicted with three valid witnesses. The reading recorded is that the surplus senders are released by the shutdown case instead of holding slots, leaving the buffer partially empty at the exit so later callers still find a free slot; occupancy is therefore not what decides the strand. I added that as counterevidence, corrected the limitation that described the buffer as never filling, extended the Fact under its own id with both receipts' indices and the removed explanation, and extended the joint history to cover the fifth revision. The defect claim, the earlier counts and the unbuffered and BatchApplyCh contrasts are unchanged, and no execution is requested.

knowledge.statement: VerifyLeader counts acknowledgements from non-voters toward a voter-sized quorum, so it can report success for an interval in which the leader has had no successful interaction with any other voter. verifyLeader registers every entry of leaderState.replState (which startStopReplication creates for every configured server except the leader itself, without consulting Suffrage) on repl.notify, so each of those peers is asked to acknowledge; a successful AppendEntries reply (updateLastAppended and the heartbeat path) or a successful InstallSnapshot replies with notifyAll(true), which calls verifyFuture.vote(true) and increments votes; the threshold compared against is quorumSize(), computed as (voters in configurations.latest)/2+1. Every other leadership-quorum test in the same package restricts eligibility to voters: checkLeaderLease skips non-voter servers in its contacted count and requestVote rejects a candidate without a vote, so the two leadership tests disagree about whose support counts.
knowledge.conditions: A leader whose latest configuration (configurations.latest) contains a server with Suffrage other than Voter, and which can still exchange AppendEntries or InstallSnapshot RPCs with that server. With three voters and one non-voter, quorumSize() is 2, so the leader's own vote plus one non-voter acknowledgement reaches the threshold.

knowledge.statement: The leader's own leadership lease is computed over voters only: checkLeaderLease counts itself plus those servers in configurations.latest whose Suffrage is Voter and whose followerReplication last contact is within LeaderLeaseTimeout, and steps down when that count is below quorumSize(). A leader therefore stops counting an unreachable voter as contacted and steps down within roughly LeaderLeaseTimeout of the last successful interaction, while a follower cannot campaign before ElectionTimeout has elapsed since it last heard from a leader.
knowledge.conditions: A configuration accepted by Config.Validate, which requires 5ms <= LeaderLeaseTimeout <= HeartbeatTimeout <= ElectionTimeout; the lease check is driven by the leader's own timer and by the last-contact times its replication goroutines record.

knowledge.statement: Runtime configuration reload enforces the same timeout bounds as initial construction: ReloadConfig applies the reloadable fields onto the current configuration and returns the error from ValidateConfig before storing it, so LeaderLeaseTimeout can never exceed HeartbeatTimeout, nor HeartbeatTimeout exceed ElectionTimeout, on a running node. A leader cannot therefore be given a longer lease than a follower's election timeout through the public reload API.
knowledge.conditions: A call to Raft.ReloadConfig on a running node with a protocol-supported configuration; the check is performed under r.confReloadMu before the new configuration is stored, and on failure the previous configuration remains in force.

knowledge.statement: LeadershipTransferToServer accepts a non-voter target and reports success without transferring leadership to it. The leader resolves the requested ID in leaderState.replState, which contains an entry for every configured server except the leader (startStopReplication creates one per server without consulting Suffrage) and only errors with 'cannot find replication state' when no entry exists. The selected target is sent TimeoutNow, which sets it to Candidate and marks candidateFromLeadershipTransfer; that flag makes runCandidate skip pre-vote, so the target sends a real RequestVote carrying the next term. A voter handling that request adopts the higher term and becomes a follower before it reaches the hasVote check, which then refuses the vote because the candidate holds no vote; the candidate therefore cannot win. When the old leader observes the higher term it steps down, the transfer goroutine's leftLeaderLoop branch responds nil, and the caller sees success. By contrast LeadershipTransfer with no explicit target picks through pickServer, which skips every server whose Suffrage is not Voter.
knowledge.conditions: Protocol version >= 3 (otherwise LeadershipTransferToServer returns ErrUnsupportedProtocol), a cluster whose latest configuration at the leader contains the named server with Suffrage other than Voter, and pre-vote enabled or disabled (the transfer path skips pre-vote either way). The named server must be reachable from the leader, otherwise the leader reports a TimeoutNow failure instead.

knowledge.statement: A leadership transfer requested for a non-voter leaves the cluster without a leader until a voter wins the next election, while the call itself has already reported success. In the observed run with HeartbeatTimeout = ElectionTimeout = LeaderLeaseTimeout = 200ms, the call returned nil, the requested non-voter was never Leader, the previous leader was sampled outside Leader state in all 1289 samples from the instant of the call, 241 samples found no leader at all (first 1ms, last 278ms after the call, about 1.4 election timeouts), the maximum term rose from 2 to 4, and a different voter held leadership at the end. The voter-target control with the same call returned nil and did hand leadership to the requested server.
knowledge.conditions: Cluster of three voters plus one non-voter joined through AddNonvoter, protocol version >= 3, all peers reachable, pre-vote left at its default, and a single process with in-memory transports; the target is chosen by its suffrage in the leader's latest configuration, not by any observed result.

knowledge.statement: Election vote solicitation is restricted to voters, unlike the verify path in the same file. electSelf and preElectSelf both iterate configurations.latest.Servers and act only when server.Suffrage == Voter: the local server records a vote for itself and every other server is asked with a RequestVote or RequestPreVote RPC, while non-voters are skipped altogether, so no non-voter grant is ever counted toward the voter-sized quorum they compare against. The grant side is not what keeps non-voters out: requestVote rejects a candidate that holds no vote and a candidate that is not in the configuration, but it imposes no suffrage requirement on the server granting, and it persists and grants a vote whenever the candidate's log is at least as up to date, so a non-voter would grant if it were asked. verifyLeader is the path that does ask every entry of leaderState.replState, which includes non-voters.
knowledge.conditions: A server whose latest configuration contains non-voting members, with pre-vote either enabled (preElectSelf) or disabled (electSelf directly); the solicitation loops read configurations.latest on the candidate's own main thread.

knowledge.statement: A follower attempts an election after HeartbeatTimeout without contact from a leader, and ElectionTimeout governs only a candidate's retry. runFollower arms heartbeatTimer with randomTimeout(HeartbeatTimeout) and campaigns when the time since last contact is at least HeartbeatTimeout, while runCandidate arms its timer with randomTimeout(ElectionTimeout) and simply restarts the election when it fires. randomTimeout(v) returns v plus a random fraction of v, so a campaign begins in [H, 2H). Correspondingly ValidateConfig requires LeaderLeaseTimeout <= HeartbeatTimeout <= ElectionTimeout, and the leader's own lease check runs every max(minCheckInterval, LeaderLeaseTimeout - maxDiff) with minCheckInterval = 10ms, stepping down at the first check whose voter contact age exceeds LeaderLeaseTimeout; the comparison is diff <= leaseTimeout, so a check at exactly the boundary still counts the voter as contacted.
knowledge.conditions: The default follower and leader loops in this snapshot, with pre-vote enabled or disabled; the numbers quoted are for a configuration accepted by ValidateConfig, and the exposure analysis assumes in-memory or low-latency RPCs.

knowledge.statement: A VerifyLeader request queued while a leader's main loop is stalled past its lease is answered without success once the stall ends, even though a successor has been elected in the meantime. Across eight trials the stalled leader held only Leader state for every 1ms sample while another server led at term 3 (first seen at 345-464ms), yet the queued verify returned non-nil in all eight: seven times 'leadership lost while committing log' and twice 'node is not the leader', at 600-602ms, the moment the stall released the main loop; the concurrent Apply failed the same way. The endpoints show the lease case was already ready when the loop resumed, so leadership was given up before the non-voter's acknowledgement could be counted, which is ordering rather than the eligibility rule that the verify quorum itself violates.

In the retained run of the three-partition probe, the leader whose only reachable peer was the non-voter returned success in 0ms while its own latest configuration reported three voters, one non-voter and a quorum size of 2, and the leader was still in Leader state (parsed event index 1); the control partition that kept one voter reachable also returned success, which shows the harness does observe a genuine acknowledgement path (index 3); the control partition with no reachable peer did not return success at all, returning 'leadership lost while committing log' after 202ms with the node in Follower state, so the leader cannot reach the threshold on its own vote and the non-voter acknowledgement is what satisfied it in the first case (index 5). All three declared comparisons hold with the setup event matched as admission (correlations 1->0, 3->2, 5->4). The source explains the mechanism: verifyLeader asks every entry of leaderState.replState to acknowledge, startStopReplication creates such an entry for every configured server except the leader without consulting Suffrage, any successful AppendEntries or InstallSnapshot reply from such a peer calls notifyAll(true) and increments verifyFuture.votes, and the threshold compared against is quorumSize(), counted over voters alone. The same package treats voter eligibility strictly in its other leadership tests: checkLeaderLease does not count a non-voter, requestVote refuses a candidate that holds no vote, and quorumSize itself counts only voters, so the verify path is the outlier rather than a deliberate relaxation. The consequence for reads stays bounded and is not what this receipt measures. The leader's lease is voter-only, and both Config.Validate and ReloadConfig enforce LeaderLeaseTimeout <= HeartbeatTimeout <= ElectionTimeout, so the old leader is normally removed before a voter majority elects a successor; the no-peer control is exactly that lease firing at 202ms with a 200ms lease. What the receipt does establish is the weaker but unconditional part: for an interval in which the leader exchanged nothing with any other voter, VerifyLeader reports success, so a caller relying on that call for read consistency is really relying on the lease timer rather than on the acknowledgements VerifyLeader collected. The same file shows the omission is not a considered relaxation of voter eligibility: electSelf and preElectSelf build the very same voter-sized threshold, and both iterate the leader's latest configuration asking only servers whose Suffrage is Voter, so a candidate neither solicits nor counts a non-voter's grant even though nothing on the granting side stops a non-voter from granting a vote if it were asked. Only the verify path asks every replication peer. That contrast is recorded as its own Behaviour so the finding is not reused without it, and it turns the question's answer from 'the success signal is weaker than its documentation' into 'the success signal contradicts the eligibility rule the same decisions use everywhere else'.

interpretations.rationale: The question asked whether a leader stalled past its lease can still answer a queued VerifyLeader with success by counting the reachable non-voter, and the execution answers no for this model. In all eight trials (parsed result events at indices 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13, 15) the intended condition was reached: the stalled leader kept Leader state for every sample (leader_not_leader_samples 0 in seven trials and 1 in one) while a different server was observed in Leader state at term 3 between 345ms and 464ms after the partition, so the cluster really did have two servers believing they led it during the stall. The queued VerifyLeader nevertheless never reported success: every endpoint was non-nil, seven trials answering 'leadership lost while committing log' and two answering 'node is not the leader', all at 600-602ms, which is exactly when the 600ms store stall released the main loop. The same run's Apply in the same window also ended with ErrLeadershipLost. The endpoints distinguish the two interleavings: 'leadership lost while committing log' is the answer the leader loop's cleanup gives to a verify it has already registered, so in those trials the verify case was served and then the runLeader defer answered it when leadership was given up, while 'node is not the leader' is the follower loop's answer to a request still queued in verifyCh, so in those trials the request never even reached verifyLeader. Neither outcome counts the non-voter's acknowledgement. The reason is ordering rather than eligibility: by the time the stall ends, the lease case is already ready, so the main loop gives up leadership in the next iteration, before the heartbeat round trip to the non-voter can return a vote. This refutes the suspicion for this route, not the parent defect: the accounting behaviour that counts a non-voter remains in the source and was observed directly in the parent question's probe. What the trial excludes is the specific consequence I was probing, namely that a stalled leader serving a queued verify hands a client a stale-read verdict. Two limits keep that exclusion narrow: it was measured with in-memory transports, where the acknowledgement round trip is far faster than the loop iteration that gives up leadership, and at eight trials it cannot bound an interleaving whose window is sub-millisecond. The parent question's gap therefore narrows to that scheduling residue rather than closing.
counterevidence: The stall model, not the source, is what the trials refute: a slower or differently placed stall could change which case the main loop serves first, and a networked deployment makes each RPC round trip orders of magnitude slower than the loop iteration, which is the opposite direction from the one that produced these endpoints.

In two trials the failure was ErrNotLeader rather than ErrLeadershipLost, showing the queued request sometimes never reached verifyLeader at all; those trials measure the queue being drained after leadership loss rather than the race between the acknowledgement and the step-down.
limitations: One execution of eight trials is cited; the endpoints were uniform (0/8 success) but the reported interleavings are inferred from the two error values, not sampled directly.

The stall is a wrapper around the log store that blocks the leader's main loop inside StoreLogs; the source comment on dispatchLogs shows the store write happens on the main thread, so the model matches that path, but a stall elsewhere (for example inside the lease check itself or a host suspension) is not covered.

interpretations.rationale: The question was whether a future handed back by VerifyLeader, Barrier or Apply while Shutdown runs can be left permanently uncompleted, and the execution answers yes for VerifyLeader. In the retained run of three shutdown trials (result events at parsed indices 1, 7 and 13) the verify cases left 9, 41 and 0 of their 64 futures uncompleted 400ms after Shutdown() had returned, with every completed call reporting success; the same call kind on a node that is never shut down completed all 64 in its control (index 19). That matches the source: VerifyLeader creates a verifyFuture and calls init(), which allocates only the error channel (future.go 99-101), leaving ShutdownCh nil, so deferError.Error() waits on errCh or on a channel that is never used (future.go 103-117). interpretations.rationale: VerifyLeader's documented role is to ensure this peer is still the leader so that stale data is not returned from the FSM. The question was whether its success establishes voter-majority contact; the execution says it does not. In the retained run of the three-partition probe, the leader whose only reachable peer was the non-voter returned success in 0ms while its own latest configuration reported three voters, one non-voter and a quorum size of 2, and the leader was still in Leader state (parsed event index 1); the control partition that kept one voter reachable also returned success, which shows the harness does observe a genuine acknowledgement path (index 3); the control partition with no reachable peer did not return success at all, returning 'leadership lost while committing log' after 202ms with the node in Follower state, so the leader cannot reach the threshold on its own vote and the non-voter acknowledgement is what satisfied it in the first case (index 5). All three declared comparisons hold with the setup event matched as admission (correlations 1->0, 3->2, 5->4). The source explains the mechanism: verifyLeader asks every entry of leaderState.replState to acknowledge, startStopReplication creates such an entry for every configured server except the leader without consulting Suffrage, any successful AppendEntries or InstallSnapshot reply from such a peer calls notifyAll(true) and increments verifyFuture.votes, and the threshold compared against is quorumSize(), counted over voters alone. The same package treats voter eligibility strictly in its other leadership tests: checkLeaderLease does not count a non-voter, requestVote refuses a candidate that holds no vote, and quorumSize itself counts only voters, so the verify path is the outlier rather than a deliberate relaxation. That contrast is recorded as its own Behaviour so the finding is not reused without it, and it turns the question's answer from 'the success signal is weaker than its documentation' into 'the success signal contradicts the eligibility rule the same decisions use everywhere else'. The consequence that this account previously kept conditional is now witnessed. A separate probe registers the verify request while the leader is isolated from every peer, stalls the leader's main loop inside StoreLogs for 900ms so its lease case cannot run, and reconnects only the non-voter once a voter majority has had time to elect. The parent defect claim is unchanged; what changes is its consequence, which is no longer conditional on an unobserved interleaving but demonstrated under a stated condition.

interpretations.rationale: The question is whether a future handed back by VerifyLeader, Barrier or Apply around Shutdown can be left permanently uncompleted, and the corrected revision now answers it with all five declared comparisons satisfied, including the two that a configuration change makes decisive. A call made after Shutdown has returned should get the documented 'raft is already shutdown' error, and that is what happens for the unbuffered call kinds: Barrier and Apply answered all eight post-shutdown calls in every trial (comparisons 2 and 3, indices 3, 9, 15 and 5, 11, 17). VerifyLeader, whose channel is always buffered, answered only 4, 4 and 5 of its eight post-shutdown calls (indices 1, 7 and 13), leaving 4, 4 and 3 futures incomplete after 500ms. With BatchApplyCh enabled - the option whose comment says it buffers applyCh to MaxAppendEntries and thereby breaks the timeout guarantee on Apply - the two unbuffered kinds flip: Barrier answered 6, 3 and 4 of eight (indices 25, 29, 33) and Apply 3, 3 and 5 (indices 27, 31, 35), leaving 11 and 13 of 24 calls stranded respectively, with roughly half of the calls in each case answered and the rest left with a future nothing will complete (comparisons 0 and 1). That is a causal rather than correlational demonstration: the only difference between the answered and the stranded cases is whether the channel a future is sent to is buffered, since the call shape, the future type and the absence of a shutdown channel on these futures are identical. The source explains the split exactly: VerifyLeader and the apply path share the same select over the shutdown channel and a channel send, verifyCh is created with 64 slots while applyCh is unbuffered unless BatchApplyCh buffers it, and none of these futures sets ShutdownCh, so deferError.Error() waits on an error channel that no surviving goroutine will write. The repository's own test file records the same class as a TODO for these calls, which is an admission that the gap was known rather than a contract that permits a caller's Error() to block forever. The earlier receipts stay part of the account: the first showed the racing form, 9 and 41 of 64 futures incomplete in two of three trials with none in the control, and the two later revisions did not reproduce that form (0 of 128 per case), so the racing variant is a timing-dependent manifestation while the post-shutdown form is stable across three executions and is the one the claim rests on. A fifth revision tested whether the strand depends on spare capacity in verifyCh by issuing 320 concurrent racing calls, five times the 64 slots, in three VerifyLeader cases (result events at parsed indices 25, 27 and 29). Over-subscription did not protect later callers: 6, 5 and 6 of the eight post-shutdown calls were answered and 2, 3 and 2 returned futures that stayed incomplete, which is the same outcome as the 128-call cases in the same run (5, 1 and 3 answered; 3, 7 and 5 stranded) and the declared comparison asking for every post-shutdown call to be answered was therefore contradicted with three valid witnesses. The reading is that the racing surplus senders are released by the shutdown case instead of holding slots, so the buffer ends partially empty at the exit and later callers still find a free slot to be accepted into; occupancy at the exit is thus not what decides the strand, and the mechanism stands as the buffered channel plus a future with no shutdown channel of its own.
counterevidence: The racing form did not reproduce in the later revisions (0 of 128 calls per case in two runs), so the earlier 9 and 41 are a timing-dependent manifestation rather than a rate.

Without BatchApplyCh the apply path is never affected: Barrier and Apply answered every post-shutdown call in all three runs (indices 3, 9, 15 and 5, 11, 17 here), so the defect reaches the apply path only under a configuration whose own comment already warns that it breaks the Apply timeout guarantee.

Roughly half of the calls in each affected case are answered with the documented shutdown error rather than stranded, so the outcome is a per-call select choice, and no call that was answered carried a wrong outcome.
The repository's test file records the same class as a known TODO, which is evidence about intent, not a reason to treat an unbounded block as acceptable.

Over-subscribing verifyCh five-fold did not remove the strand: the 320-call cases stranded 2, 3 and 2 of eight post-shutdown calls, against 3, 7 and 5 of eight for the 128-call cases, so the outcome is not decided by spare capacity being available when the loop exits.
limitations: The post-shutdown counts per case come from three trials of eight calls each (VerifyLeader 11 of 24 stranded; batched Barrier 11 of 24; batched Apply 13 of 24), so they bound the mechanism rather than a population rate.
The strand is classified by a 500ms window; permanence is inferred from the source, since no reader of the affected channel remains and these futures carry no shutdown channel.

The over-subscribed cases carry 320 concurrent racing calls, five times the 64 verifyCh slots, so a large share of sends could not be accepted; the buffer still ended with free slots and the strand persisted, which means occupancy at the exit is not what the probe controls.
